ownerIntake.ownerGoal: Lift in-account active adoption back above 60%, restore NRR above 115% via seat expansion, and simplify the product; reach $20M ARR within 15 months to support a Series C.
ownerConstraints: Funding constraint: $90M raised, 28-month runway; Series C is gated on NRR and net-new seat expansion, both of which depend on in-account adoption.

Product constraint: feature count tripled in two years; the UI is cluttered and core workflows are buried. Simplifying the experience (progressive disclosure, role-based defaults, guided core workflows) is a 10-14 week product+design effort; ripping out features risks enterprise contractual dependencies.

Organizational constraint: 130 staff (40 engineering, weighted toward feature delivery; 22 product/design; 24 sales; 20 CS; rest G&A). Product culture has rewarded shipping features over adoption outcomes.
Market constraint: competitors range from simpler point tools to broad suites; the company wins on breadth at purchase but loses daily-use engagement to simpler tools inside the same accounts.

Commercial constraint: expansion revenue depends on growing active seats; when only 38% of licensed seats are active, accounts will not buy more seats, and renewals at flat or reduced seat counts loom.

businessProblem: A collaboration SaaS growing 45% is seeing its expansion engine seize because users stop using the product. In-account active adoption (weekly active / licensed seats) fell from 62% to 38% over 18 months while feature count tripled; NRR fell 118%→104% as seat expansion stalled; support tickets per seat rose 55% with 'too complicated' (34%) and 'can't find feature' (28%) as top themes. Power users (top 15%) stay highly engaged, but the broad licensed base disengages, and new seats reach active use only 29% of the time within 60 days. The owner suspects simplicity and expansion problems and weighs both a simplification effort and new expansion features (the cultural default of shipping). The real pattern is a usability/trust failure inside accounts: feature bloat buries core workflows (median clicks-to-core-task up 40%; 11 of 60+ features drive 80% of usage), so non-power users abandon the product, trust in daily use erodes, and seat expansion becomes impossible. With Series C gated on NRR/seat expansion and 28 months of runway, the owner must decide whether to keep shipping features or fix the in-account adoption/trust failure.

evidence.finding: In-account active adoption collapsed from 62% to 38% of licensed seats active (weekly) over 18 months, and new licensed seats reach active use only 29% of the time within 60 days. Power users (top 15%) remain highly engaged, but the broad licensed base disengages, indicating a complexity barrier that affects non-power users specifically.
evidence.source: Product usage analytics (active seats / licensed seats), cohort activation tracking

evidence.finding: Feature bloat has degraded usability: feature count tripled in two years, median clicks-to-core-task rose 40%, and just 11 of 60+ shipped features account for 80% of active usage. Core workflows are buried under rarely-used features, making the product harder to use for the broad base.
evidence.source: Product telemetry (clicks-to-task, feature usage distribution), design audit

evidence.finding: NRR fell from 118% to 104% over 12 months as seat expansion stalled, while gross retention stayed healthy at 96%. The decline is driven by failure to expand seats, which is impossible when only 38% of licensed seats are active. Accounts will not buy more seats they cannot get users to adopt.
evidence.source: NRR cohort report, seat-expansion bookings analysis

evidence.finding: Support tickets per seat are up 55%, with top themes 'too complicated' (34%) and 'can't find feature' (28%). The friction is usability and discoverability, not capability gaps or reliability outages, which localizes the problem to product complexity eroding daily-use trust.
evidence.source: Support ticket analytics with theme coding

evidence.finding: Competitors range from simpler point tools to broad suites. The company wins on breadth at purchase but loses daily-use engagement to simpler tools inside the same accounts, where employees gravitate to easier alternatives for routine work. The competitive threat is in-account usage share, not deal-stage capability.
